A_target.statement:
Let $\mathbf A$ be a [[Definition:Square Matrix|square matrix]] over a [[Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)|field]] $K$.
Then its [[Definition:Minimal Polynomial of Matrix|minimal polynomial]] $m_{\mathbf A}$ divides its [[Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Matrix|characteristic polynomial]] $p_{\mathbf A}$, and they have the same roots in $K$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over a commutative ring.
Then $\map {p_{\mathbf A} } {\mathbf A} = \mathbf 0$.

substitutions.the annihilating polynomial p_A: an element of the ideal of polynomials vanishing at A

object_map.reformulation: Collect all annihilating polynomials into an ideal of the principal ideal domain K[t].

validity_conditions: K[t] must be a principal ideal domain, which holds as K is a field.
The converse inclusion of roots uses an eigenvector.
proof_plan:
Let $I = \set {f \in K \sqbrk t: \map f {\mathbf A} = \mathbf 0}$.
As $\map {\paren {f + g} } {\mathbf A} = \map f {\mathbf A} + \map g {\mathbf A}$ and $\map {\paren {f g} } {\mathbf A} = \map f {\mathbf A} \map g {\mathbf A}$, $I$ is an [[Definition:Ideal of Ring|ideal]].
As $K \sqbrk t$ is a [[Definition:Principal Ideal Domain|principal ideal domain]], $I = \ideal {m_{\mathbf A} }$ for a unique monic $m_{\mathbf A}$, the minimal polynomial.

By the [[Cayley-Hamilton Theorem]], $p_{\mathbf A} \in I$, so $m_{\mathbf A} \divides p_{\mathbf A}$.
Hence every root of $m_{\mathbf A}$ is a root of $p_{\mathbf A}$.

Conversely, if $\mathbf A \mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$ with $\mathbf v \ne \mathbf 0$, then $\mathbf 0 = \map {m_{\mathbf A} } {\mathbf A} \mathbf v = \map {m_{\mathbf A} } \lambda \mathbf v$, so $\map {m_{\mathbf A} } \lambda = 0$.
{{qed}}
